# Kalman Filtering and the Extended Kalman Filter {#sec-ekf}

The Bayes filter gives the exact recursive structure, but exact belief
distributions are usually too expensive to maintain. The Kalman filter makes
the problem practical by assuming the belief is Gaussian and the models are
linear with additive Gaussian noise.

That sounds restrictive because it is. It is also one of the most useful
approximations in navigation.

This chapter starts with the linear Kalman filter, then extends it to nonlinear
systems through local linearization. The final section connects the EKF idea to
error-state inertial navigation, where the filter estimates small errors rather
than the full navigation state directly.

## Linear Gaussian Systems {#sec-ekf-linear-gaussian-systems}

The discrete-time linear system model is

$$
\mathbf{x}_k =
\mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{x}_{k-1}
+
\mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{u}_k
+
\mathbf{w}_k,
\qquad
\mathbf{w}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_k),
$$

with measurement model

$$
\mathbf{z}_k =
\mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{x}_k
+
\mathbf{v}_k,
\qquad
\mathbf{v}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R}_k).
$$

The state belief is represented by a mean and covariance:

$$
\mathbf{x}_{k-1}
\sim
\mathcal{N}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1}, \mathbf{P}_{k-1}).
$$

The symbols have standard roles:

- $\mathbf{F}_k$ propagates the state.
- $\mathbf{B}_k$ maps known inputs into the state.
- $\mathbf{Q}_k$ describes process noise and unmodeled dynamics.
- $\mathbf{H}_k$ maps state into measurement space.
- $\mathbf{R}_k$ describes measurement noise.

If these assumptions are true, the Kalman filter is the exact Bayes filter for
the linear Gaussian system.

## Prediction {#sec-ekf-prediction}

The predicted state mean is

$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k^-
=
\mathbf{F}_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1}
+
\mathbf{B}_k \mathbf{u}_k.
$$

The predicted covariance is

$$
\mathbf{P}_k^-
=
\mathbf{F}_k \mathbf{P}_{k-1} \mathbf{F}_k^T
+
\mathbf{Q}_k.
$$

The covariance equation says two things at once. First, uncertainty is
transformed by the dynamics. Second, new uncertainty enters through process
noise. If $\mathbf{Q}_k$ is too small, the filter becomes overconfident and may
reject valid measurements. If $\mathbf{Q}_k$ is too large, the filter will
wander around and let measurements dominate.

## Measurement Update {#sec-ekf-measurement-update}

The innovation is the difference between the actual measurement and the
predicted measurement:

$$
\mathbf{y}_k
=
\mathbf{z}_k - \mathbf{H}_k \hat{\mathbf{x}}_k^-.
$$

The innovation covariance is

$$
\mathbf{S}_k
=
\mathbf{H}_k \mathbf{P}_k^- \mathbf{H}_k^T + \mathbf{R}_k.
$$

The Kalman gain is

$$
\mathbf{K}_k
=
\mathbf{P}_k^- \mathbf{H}_k^T \mathbf{S}_k^{-1}.
$$

Then the posterior state and covariance are

$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k
=
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k^- + \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{y}_k,
$$

$$
\mathbf{P}_k
=
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)\mathbf{P}_k^-.
$$

In software, prefer solving the linear system for the gain rather than forming
an explicit matrix inverse. For numerical robustness, the Joseph covariance
update is often better:

$$
\mathbf{P}_k
=
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)
\mathbf{P}_k^-
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}_k)^T
+
\mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{R}_k \mathbf{K}_k^T.
$$

It is a few more matrix multiplies, but it is less likely to destroy symmetry
or positive semidefiniteness through roundoff.

## Kalman Gain Intuition {#sec-ekf-kalman-gain-intuition}

In a scalar measurement problem, the gain is

$$
K = \frac{P^-}{P^- + R}.
$$

If measurement noise $R$ is small, $K$ approaches one and the filter trusts the
measurement. If $R$ is large, $K$ approaches zero and the filter trusts the
prediction.

::: {#cell-fig-kalman-gain-noise .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

R_values = np.logspace(-3, 2, 500)
predicted_variances = [0.05, 0.2, 1.0, 5.0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
for P_minus in predicted_variances:
    gain = P_minus / (P_minus + R_values)
    ax.semilogx(R_values, gain, label=fr"$P^-={P_minus}$")

ax.set_xlabel("measurement variance R")
ax.set_ylabel("Kalman gain K")
ax.set_title("Measurement trust decreases as measurement noise increases")
ax.grid(True, which="both", alpha=0.25)
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Scalar Kalman gain as measurement noise changes. Larger predicted uncertainty increases measurement influence; larger measurement noise decreases it.](ekf_files/figure-html/fig-kalman-gain-noise-output-1.png){#fig-kalman-gain-noise width=663 height=377}
:::
:::


The gain is not a magic tuning knob. It is the consequence of the uncertainty
model. If the gain seems wrong, inspect $\mathbf{P}^-$ and $\mathbf{R}$ before
you start sprinkling constants into the code.

## A Constant-Velocity Example {#sec-ekf-constant-velocity-example}

For 1D motion with position $s$ and velocity $\dot{s}$,

$$
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
s \\
\dot{s}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If acceleration $a$ is treated as a known input over one time step $\Delta t$,
the discrete model is

$$
\mathbf{x}_k
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & \Delta t \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}_{k-1}
+
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{2}\Delta t^2 \\
\Delta t
\end{bmatrix}
a_k
+
\mathbf{w}_k.
$$

If the sensor measures position only,

$$
z_k =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\mathbf{x}_k
+
v_k.
$$

A minimal implementation follows the equations directly:

::: {#kalman-constant-velocity-code .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np


def kalman_predict(x, P, F, B, u, Q):
    x_bar = F @ x + B @ u
    P_bar = F @ P @ F.T + Q
    return x_bar, P_bar


def kalman_update(x_bar, P_bar, z, H, R):
    innovation = z - H @ x_bar
    S = H @ P_bar @ H.T + R
    K = np.linalg.solve(S.T, (P_bar @ H.T).T).T
    x = x_bar + K @ innovation
    I = np.eye(P_bar.shape[0])
    P = (I - K @ H) @ P_bar @ (I - K @ H).T + K @ R @ K.T
    return x, P, innovation, S
```
:::


This is the basic pattern behind many navigation filters. The state and matrix
dimensions grow, but the loop remains prediction, innovation, gain, correction.

## Continuous Models and Discretization {#sec-ekf-continuous-models-discretization}

Real motion is continuous. Digital filters run at discrete time steps. A common
continuous-time linear model is

$$
\dot{\mathbf{x}}(t)
=
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}(t)
+
\mathbf{B}\mathbf{u}(t)
+
\mathbf{G}\mathbf{w}(t).
$$

For small time steps, one-step Euler integration gives

$$
\mathbf{F}
\approx
\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A}\Delta t.
$$

For some simple systems, the exact discretization is easy. The constant-velocity
model has

$$
\mathbf{A}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 \\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{F}
=
\exp(\mathbf{A}\Delta t)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & \Delta t \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If acceleration noise with variance $\sigma_a^2$ is modeled as constant over
the interval and enters through

$$
\mathbf{G}_d
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{2}\Delta t^2 \\
\Delta t
\end{bmatrix},
$$

then a simple discrete process covariance is

$$
\mathbf{Q}
=
\mathbf{G}_d \sigma_a^2 \mathbf{G}_d^T
=
\sigma_a^2
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{1}{4}\Delta t^4 & \frac{1}{2}\Delta t^3 \\
\frac{1}{2}\Delta t^3 & \Delta t^2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This is not the only valid noise model. The important point is that
$\mathbf{Q}$ should reflect how uncertainty enters the state, not just be a
small diagonal matrix because the code needed one.

## Why the Linear Kalman Filter Breaks {#sec-ekf-why-linear-kalman}

The linear Kalman filter relies on two assumptions:

- the process and measurement models are linear;
- the relevant uncertainties are well represented by Gaussians.

Navigation rarely gives us that much kindness. A ground robot's global position
depends on heading through sine and cosine. A landmark range measurement depends
on Euclidean distance. A bearing wraps around at $\pm \pi$. Attitude lives on a
rotation group, not in ordinary Euclidean coordinates. None of this is linear.

The Extended Kalman Filter keeps the Gaussian belief but replaces nonlinear
models with local linear approximations.

## Nonlinear System Model {#sec-ekf-nonlinear-system-model}

The nonlinear process and measurement models are

$$
\mathbf{x}_k
=
f(\mathbf{x}_{k-1}, \mathbf{u}_k) + \mathbf{w}_k,
\qquad
\mathbf{w}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_k),
$$

$$
\mathbf{z}_k
=
h(\mathbf{x}_k) + \mathbf{v}_k,
\qquad
\mathbf{v}_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{R}_k).
$$

The EKF evaluates the nonlinear functions directly for the mean, but propagates
the covariance through first-order Taylor approximations.

For the process model,

$$
f(\mathbf{x})
\approx
f(\hat{\mathbf{x}})
+
\mathbf{F}
(\mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}),
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{F}
=
\left.
\frac{\partial f}{\partial \mathbf{x}}
\right|_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}, \mathbf{u}}.
$$

For the measurement model,

$$
h(\mathbf{x})
\approx
h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}^-)
+
\mathbf{H}
(\mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}^-),
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{H}
=
\left.
\frac{\partial h}{\partial \mathbf{x}}
\right|_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}^-}.
$$

## EKF Prediction {#sec-ekf-prediction-2}

The EKF prediction is

$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k^-
=
f(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1}, \mathbf{u}_k),
$$

$$
\mathbf{P}_k^-
=
\mathbf{F}_k
\mathbf{P}_{k-1}
\mathbf{F}_k^T
+
\mathbf{Q}_k.
$$

The nonlinear function moves the mean. The Jacobian moves the covariance.

## EKF Update {#sec-ekf-update}

The innovation is

$$
\mathbf{y}_k
=
\mathbf{z}_k - h(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k^-).
$$

The innovation covariance is

$$
\mathbf{S}_k
=
\mathbf{H}_k
\mathbf{P}_k^-
\mathbf{H}_k^T
+
\mathbf{R}_k.
$$

The gain and correction are

$$
\mathbf{K}_k
=
\mathbf{P}_k^-
\mathbf{H}_k^T
\mathbf{S}_k^{-1},
$$

$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k
=
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k^-
+
\mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{y}_k.
$$

The covariance update can again use the Joseph form:

$$
\mathbf{P}_k
=
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{H}_k)
\mathbf{P}_k^-
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{H}_k)^T
+
\mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{R}_k\mathbf{K}_k^T.
$$

## Example: Range to a Landmark {#sec-ekf-example-range-landmark}

For a 2D state

$$
\mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
x & y & v_x & v_y
\end{bmatrix}^T,
$$

the range to a known landmark $\mathbf{m} = [m_x, m_y]^T$ is

$$
h(\mathbf{x})
=
\sqrt{(m_x - x)^2 + (m_y - y)^2}.
$$

Let

$$
r = \sqrt{(m_x - x)^2 + (m_y - y)^2}.
$$

The measurement Jacobian is

$$
\mathbf{H}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{x - m_x}{r}
&
\frac{y - m_y}{r}
&
0
&
0
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The zero columns matter. This measurement does not directly observe velocity,
but it can still reduce velocity uncertainty if position and velocity are
correlated in $\mathbf{P}$.

::: {#cell-fig-ekf-linearization-error .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

landmark = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
y_fixed = 2.0
x_values = np.linspace(0.2, 7.0, 500)

def range_measurement(x_position):
    dx = x_position - landmark[0]
    dy = y_fixed - landmark[1]
    return np.sqrt(dx**2 + dy**2)

x0 = 3.0
r0 = range_measurement(x0)
drdx0 = (x0 - landmark[0]) / r0
linearized = r0 + drdx0 * (x_values - x0)
true_range = range_measurement(x_values)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.plot(x_values, true_range, label="true range")
ax.plot(x_values, linearized, linestyle="--", label="first-order approximation")
ax.axvline(x0, color="0.4", linestyle=":", label="linearization point")
ax.set_xlabel("candidate x position [m], with y = 2 m")
ax.set_ylabel("range to landmark [m]")
ax.set_title("EKF measurement linearization is local")
ax.grid(True, alpha=0.25)
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![First-order EKF linearization of a nonlinear range measurement. The approximation is good near the linearization point and degrades as the state moves away.](ekf_files/figure-html/fig-ekf-linearization-error-output-1.png){#fig-ekf-linearization-error width=651 height=376}
:::
:::


This figure is the EKF's central bargain. Near the current estimate, the
linearization may be excellent. Far away, it may be misleading. If the estimate
is already wrong enough, the EKF can confidently walk itself away from the
truth.

## Computing Jacobians {#sec-ekf-computing-jacobians}

Analytical Jacobians are usually preferred when the model is small and stable.
They are fast, exact for the written model, and make the coupling between states
visible. Numerical Jacobians are useful for testing and for models that are
awkward to differentiate by hand.

::: {#ekf-jacobian-check-code .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np


def range_to_landmark(state, landmark):
    dx = state[0] - landmark[0]
    dy = state[1] - landmark[1]
    return np.array([np.sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy)])


def range_jacobian(state, landmark):
    dx = state[0] - landmark[0]
    dy = state[1] - landmark[1]
    r = np.sqrt(dx * dx + dy * dy)
    return np.array([[dx / r, dy / r, 0.0, 0.0]])


def numerical_jacobian(func, x, eps=1e-6):
    y0 = func(x)
    J = np.zeros((y0.size, x.size))
    for i in range(x.size):
        x_perturbed = x.copy()
        x_perturbed[i] += eps
        J[:, i] = (func(x_perturbed) - y0) / eps
    return J


state = np.array([3.0, 2.0, 0.5, -0.1])
landmark = np.array([0.0, 0.0])

H_analytical = range_jacobian(state, landmark)
H_numerical = numerical_jacobian(lambda s: range_to_landmark(s, landmark), state)

np.testing.assert_allclose(H_analytical, H_numerical, atol=1e-5)
```
:::


Do not treat finite differences as a substitute for understanding the model.
They are a good smoke test. They are not a license to ignore singularities,
angle wrapping, units, or frame conventions.

## Consistency Checks {#sec-ekf-consistency-checks}

An EKF can produce reasonable-looking state estimates while its covariance is
wrong. Consistency checks compare residual behavior against the uncertainty the
filter claims to have.

The normalized innovation squared is

$$
\epsilon_k
=
\mathbf{y}_k^T
\mathbf{S}_k^{-1}
\mathbf{y}_k.
$$

For a correct linear Gaussian model, $\epsilon_k$ follows a chi-square
distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the measurement dimension. In
practice, we use this as a diagnostic, not as a sacred contract.

Large innovations can mean:

- the state estimate is wrong;
- the measurement is an outlier;
- the measurement covariance is too optimistic;
- the wrong feature was associated with the measurement;
- the linearization point is poor;
- the model is missing real physics.

The EKF is not fragile because it uses matrices. It is fragile because it is
very good at hiding bad modeling assumptions behind clean matrices.

## Practical Implementation Considerations {#sec-ekf-practical-implementation-considerations}

The Kalman and Extended Kalman filters are simple on paper. Most implementation
failures come from numerical linear algebra, state representation, or bad
linearization.

Use the Joseph covariance update unless there is a measured reason not to:

$$
\mathbf{P}_k
=
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{H}_k)
\mathbf{P}_k^-
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{H}_k)^T
+
\mathbf{K}_k\mathbf{R}_k\mathbf{K}_k^T.
$$

The simpler update $(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{K}\mathbf{H})\mathbf{P}^-$ is
algebraically equivalent under exact arithmetic, but software does not run on
exact arithmetic. The Joseph form is more robust against loss of symmetry and
small negative eigenvalues.

Avoid explicit matrix inverses. Compute gains and consistency metrics with
linear solves:

::: {#ekf-linear-solve-code .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np


def kalman_gain(P_bar: np.ndarray, H: np.ndarray, R: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    S = H @ P_bar @ H.T + R
    return np.linalg.solve(S.T, (P_bar @ H.T).T).T


def normalized_innovation_squared(y: np.ndarray, S: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(y.T @ np.linalg.solve(S, y))
```
:::


Keep covariance matrices symmetric. After an update, it is reasonable to enforce
symmetry at machine precision and check positive semidefiniteness:

::: {#ekf-covariance-check-code .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np


def symmetrize_covariance(P: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    return 0.5 * (P + P.T)


def assert_covariance_is_reasonable(P: np.ndarray, tolerance: float = 1e-10) -> None:
    eigvals = np.linalg.eigvalsh(symmetrize_covariance(P))
    if np.min(eigvals) < -tolerance:
        raise ValueError(f"covariance is not positive semidefinite: min eigenvalue {eigvals.min()}")
```
:::


Prefer analytical Jacobians for production when they are tractable, but test
them against numerical Jacobians. Numerical Jacobians are useful as checks and
prototypes; they are sensitive to step size, scaling, discontinuities, and angle
wrapping.

Finally, treat angles and attitude states explicitly. Innovations involving
angles should be wrapped into the correct interval before applying the update.
For 3D attitude, use an error-state or manifold-aware representation rather than
pretending Euler angles behave nicely everywhere.

## Error-State Filtering {#sec-ekf-error-state-filtering}

Many inertial navigation systems use an error-state Kalman filter rather than a
full-state EKF. The nominal navigation state is propagated by the inertial
mechanization equations:

$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_\text{nominal}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\hat{\mathbf{p}} &
\hat{\mathbf{v}} &
\hat{\mathbf{R}} &
\hat{\mathbf{b}}_g &
\hat{\mathbf{b}}_a
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The filter state is a small perturbation:

$$
\delta \mathbf{x}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\delta \mathbf{p} &
\delta \mathbf{v} &
\delta \boldsymbol{\theta} &
\delta \mathbf{b}_g &
\delta \mathbf{b}_a
\end{bmatrix}^T.
$$

The relationship is

$$
\mathbf{x}
=
\hat{\mathbf{x}}_\text{nominal}
\boxplus
\delta \mathbf{x},
$$

where $\boxplus$ means "apply the error to the nominal state." For ordinary
position and velocity this is addition. For attitude it is a small rotation
applied to the nominal orientation.

The workflow is:

1. Propagate the nominal state with IMU measurements.
2. Propagate the error covariance with linearized error dynamics.
3. Use external measurements, such as GNSS position or velocity, to estimate the
   error state.
4. Inject the estimated error into the nominal state.
5. Reset the error-state mean to zero while keeping the corrected covariance.

This works well because many inertial navigation errors are small and locally
linear even though the full attitude and position dynamics are nonlinear. It
also keeps the attitude representation on the correct geometric object instead
of pretending Euler angles are harmless everywhere.

## INS/GNSS Bridge {#sec-ekf-ins-gnss-bridge}

In loosely coupled INS/GNSS integration, the inertial navigation solution is
propagated at high rate using IMU data, while GNSS provides slower position or
velocity updates. A simple measurement model might be

$$
\mathbf{z}_\text{GNSS}
=
\hat{\mathbf{p}}_\text{INS}
+
\delta \mathbf{p}
+
\mathbf{v}_\text{GNSS}.
$$

In error-state form, the innovation is approximately

$$
\mathbf{y}
=
\mathbf{z}_\text{GNSS} - \hat{\mathbf{p}}_\text{INS}
\approx
\delta \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}_\text{GNSS}.
$$

The measurement matrix simply selects the position-error portion of the error
state:

$$
\mathbf{H}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{I}_{3 \times 3} &
\mathbf{0}_{3 \times 3} &
\mathbf{0}_{3 \times 3} &
\mathbf{0}_{3 \times 3} &
\mathbf{0}_{3 \times 3}
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The full implementation becomes more involved once Earth rotation, transport
rate, gravity, lever arms, time synchronization, and attitude error definitions
are included. The important filtering idea is simple: use the high-rate inertial
system for propagation and slower external measurements to bound drift.

## When the EKF Is a Good Choice {#sec-ekf-when-ekf-good}

The EKF is a good practical filter when:

- the belief is mostly unimodal;
- the estimate is usually close enough that local linearization is valid;
- analytical or tested numerical Jacobians are available;
- measurement models are differentiable in the operating region;
- the system needs the speed and memory efficiency of a Gaussian filter.

The EKF is a poor fit when:

- the posterior is strongly multimodal;
- the initial estimate can be far from the truth;
- the models have hard discontinuities;
- data association is highly ambiguous;
- angle wrapping or attitude parameterization is handled casually.

The EKF is popular because it is effective, not because it is forgiving.

## Algorithm Summary {#sec-ekf-algorithm-summary}

For each time step:

```text
predict:
    x_bar = f(x, u)
    F = df/dx evaluated at the previous estimate
    P_bar = F P F.T + Q

update:
    y = z - h(x_bar)
    H = dh/dx evaluated at x_bar
    S = H P_bar H.T + R
    K = P_bar H.T inv(S)
    x = x_bar + K y
    P = Joseph covariance update
```

The notation is compact. The real work is in choosing the state, models,
frames, noise parameters, and consistency checks well enough that these
equations mean what we think they mean.
